title: Making Your Mind Up

paragraphs.text: Human beings make hundreds of decisions every day regarding work, diet, health, shopping and numerous other aspects of life. The idea that people's decision-making and subsequent behaviour can be influenced in subtle ways is known generally as behavioural economies. One example would be Nudge theory, which is fashionable in business circles partly because it has the backing of psychologists and neuroscientists. The principles of Nudge theory have recently been applied by a bank in New Zealand.For at least 20 years, both local and international financial experts have been warning New Zealanders that they should save more for retirement, with limited success. So one of the country's banks, Kiwibank, came up with the Future You campaign, whereby online tools provided each customer with a detailed analysis of how much money people would need in their retirement. Almost immediately, customers started to save more, when the earlier warnings of financial experts had had little effect. This demonstrates one of the principles of Nudge theory which is that showing people is better than telling them. Given this difference, Kiwibank's approach ought now to become the standard for its competitors. However, behavioural economics is increasingly showing that decision-making is a complex process.

Recently, the business consultancy TRA set out to prove just how little is actually known about why people make certain choices. TRA wanted to show their client, the DB drinks company, that asking people why they bought certain drinks was unproductive. To demonstrate, they asked shoppers to explain their preferences and then set up cameras in a store. This is a well-established technique used in research and one that often provides reliable evidence. In this case, the preferences shoppers expressed bore no resemblance to what they actually bought in the store. In fact, their in-store decisions seemed to be affected most by factors such as the layout of the shop and other aspects of its environment.

The principles of behavioural economics don't just apply to finance and consumer decision-making. They can relate more widely to people's lives and how they make all sorts of decisions. These principles, for example, have been used to create The Journal, a website designed to support those suffering from stress and anxiety. Based on input from the medical community, the site employs a famous sports star to advise its users to slow down and limit their expectations. For example, they should only try to modify their behaviour in small ways, like deciding to eat healthy food twice weekly, a concept known as 'chunking. According to programme creator Simon Sievert, these sorts of behaviour alterations cannot be rushed and are only effective over the long term. Because of this, Sievert says that society should not be concerned that knowledge gained by this area of science puts too much power into the hands of corporations and even governments. In reality, he argues, manipulating people's choices and actions is much harder than it sounds because it is such an extended process.

Another important area is online activity, where constant attempts are made to influence human decision-making and behaviour. Tourism New Zealand recently partnered with Nikon to produce 360^{\circ} videos for use in its online advertising. This came from the insight that still photographs can be edited to make them more attractive. However, potential visitors would put greater trust in videos because they believe videos are harder to alter, resulting in a more effective advertising campaign. At the other extreme are social media algorithms, which use software programmes to control what viewers see. This practice on social media should be limited if we are to maintain our belief in the internet as an open and reliable platform, particularly when it comes to reporting news and current affairs.

Another insight into behavioural economics is found on the New York Times website, which in effect invites potential subscribers to join our club'. These advertisers are trying to attract people by highlighting characteristics they have in common, such as shared political beliefs. Marketing lecturer Sommer Kapitan says behavioural economics recognises the importance of a sense of community. To illustrate, she points to the growing trend for free restaurants', where customers pay what they can afford. Interestingly, most still pay something because they want to be seen as part of a neighbourhood or network where everyone contributes to help fellow members.

Then there are digital devices that count your steps or measure calorie intake. These are intended to improve decision-making and behaviour around exercise and dieting. According to Stanford University psychologist BJ Fogg, however, both devices can be counterproductive. That is because these clever devices may indicate the user is failing to achieve their goals, creating negative thoughts towards all exercise or dieting. After years of behavioural research, Fogg favours setting small, achievable targets that can be measured without the use of any digital device.

London design agency Maynard is also applying behavioural economics. One Maynard project involves placing signs at new bus and train stations to assist travellers in getting to the right location. What is truly remarkable is that putting up a sign giving directions seems simple but turns out to be such a complicated process involving the psychology of'slow' and 'fast' spaces. In a slow space, people can see a choice of directions coming and are actively looking for signs, so these need to be obvious with no distracting advertisements. In a fast space, they already know where they are going so people have the mental space to take in the advertisements around them, which might then influence their consumer decision-making. Most of us are unable to look for directions and focus on advertisements simultaneously. Such insights are further evidence of the complexity of human decision-making, and thus the potential for behavioural economics.
